sections.text: The Committee is correct that this section presents a genuine policy tradeoff and not merely a disagreement over emphasis. I agree that FCCPS policy must protect student learning and assessment integrity, and I also agree that current evidence does not justify careless or unchecked adoption of generative AI in schools. Recent research and policy guidance support caution: Brookings concluded that, at this stage, the risks of generative AI in children’s education outweigh its benefits, and Virginia’s statewide guidance stresses both “do no harm” and “augment, not replace humans.” At the same time, neither source supports a purely prohibition-based posture. Brookings also argues for holistic AI literacy and well-designed tools that teach rather than tell, while Virginia’s guidance explicitly calls for innovation, experimentation, and equitable access alongside guardrails. In my view, those sources point toward a design-first posture, not a restriction-first default. FCCPS should begin with learning goals, developmental needs, and human-accountability requirements, then decide where AI use should be permitted, structured, or restricted. (Brookings)

A restriction-first posture is understandable, and I take its concerns seriously. The strongest case for it is that harms to independent thinking, assessment validity, and student self-trust are already visible, while benefits remain uneven and context-dependent. I share those concerns. But I do not believe they justify making broader adoption a categorically secondary priority until benefits are proven in advance across all use cases. The more realistic and educationally responsible approach is to distinguish among contexts. Some uses should indeed be restricted or prohibited because they undermine core learning objectives. Other uses should be bounded, teacher-guided, and closely monitored. Still others should be explored through pilots and carefully governed classroom practice where they support AI literacy, responsible use, and student preparation for a rapidly changing environment. (Brookings)

My position, therefore, is that FCCPS should adopt a design-first posture. That means protecting assessment validity primarily through assessment design, human review, process expectations, and instructional clarity, while using restrictions where those measures are insufficient. It also means recognizing that AI literacy includes learning when not to use AI. A design-first posture is not permissive by default. It is more demanding than either uncritical adoption or blanket prohibition, because it requires FCCPS to be explicit about educational purpose, developmental appropriateness, and accountability.

heading_path: Pragmatic constraints on restriction of GenAI applications
sections.text: Any serious policy in this area must begin with enforcement reality. AI use is already occurring outside school-controlled environments, and in unproctored contexts FCCPS cannot rely on prohibition alone to create fair or consistent outcomes. Policies that depend mainly on detection or blanket bans are likely to be unevenly enforced and may create incentives for concealment rather than honesty. The Committee’s own Meeting 4 packet reflects this reality by treating the central validity question as a choice between “design/process evidence first” and “restriction-first in high-stakes,” while also advancing a risk rubric, a guidance library, advisory-only detection, and guardrailed drafting as surrounding governance tools. That combination suggests that differentiated design and governance are necessary even for those who favor stronger restrictions in some settings.

heading_path: Pragmatic constraints on restriction of GenAI applications
sections.text: There are also practical limits on how much summative work can be moved into proctored settings. Proctored environments are sometimes the right answer and should be used more intentionally for tasks where unaided performance is central to the learning objective. But they are not a complete answer. Overreliance on proctoring can narrow assignment design, increase workload, and shift rather than solve the underlying challenge of how students learn in an AI-rich world. FCCPS should therefore use proctoring selectively, where it is instructionally justified, while also redesigning assignments so that prohibited AI uses are less educationally useful and less attractive. That is a more sustainable response than trying to police every possible misuse after the fact.

heading_path: Pragmatic constraints on restriction of GenAI applications
sections.text: Trust is another practical constraint. FCCPS should protect students from two unfair conditions at once: competing against rampant non-transparent AI use by peers, and being falsely accused based on weak or opaque evidence. The Committee has already recognized broad concern about detector reliability and fairness. I agree that detectors should not be treated as primary enforcement tools and should never serve as sole evidence. A policy posture built too heavily on suspicion risks harming the student-teacher relationship that the Committee has repeatedly identified as central to learning. Design-first policy is not trust without verification; it is trust supported by clearer expectations, better assessment design, proportionate disclosure, and human review.

heading_path: Pragmatic constraints on restriction of GenAI applications
sections.text: Restriction-first policy also has an equity problem if it is not accompanied by meaningful in-school opportunities for guided AI literacy. Recent reporting on Anthropic data suggests that the gap may not be simply between AI users and non-users, but between experienced users and newcomers. If that pattern holds, then students with more access, practice, and adult support outside school will continue building fluency even if FCCPS adopts a more restrictive posture inside school. In that environment, a school-only restriction strategy can unintentionally widen differences in preparation rather than narrow them. That does not mean FCCPS should rush into broad adoption. It does mean the district should not assume that less in-school exposure is always the safer or more equitable long-term choice. (Axios)

For these reasons, I support the Committee’s conclusion that FCCPS should steer between two extremes: unchecked adoption and impractical overrestriction. I would state that posture more affirmatively as follows: FCCPS should adopt a guardrailed, design-first approach to AI integration. Under this approach, restrictions remain necessary in higher-risk contexts, especially where independent reasoning, authorship, fairness, privacy, or developmental protection are central. But those restrictions should be targeted, intelligible, and tied to clear educational purposes. Outside those contexts, FCCPS should create structured opportunities for students and educators to build AI literacy and responsible habits under human-centered rules and with appropriate safeguards. (Virginia Department of Education)

In practical terms, that means FCCPS should prefer the following sequence. First, define the learning goal and determine whether the task is one in which unaided human performance is educationally essential. Second, design the assignment, assessment conditions, and disclosure expectations accordingly. Third, determine whether AI use in that context should be prohibited, conditionally allowed, or affirmatively supported. Fourth, review outcomes over time and revise policy where evidence shows either harm or benefit. This sequence is more faithful to the Committee’s values than beginning with a broad presumption either for or against use. It is also more consistent with the Committee’s repeated emphasis on human accountability, developmental appropriateness, transparency, equity, and adaptability under uncertainty.

My respectful disagreement with a restriction-first default is therefore not a disagreement about the seriousness of current risks. It is a disagreement about what posture is most likely to protect students while preparing them well. The better path is not to normalize AI use, and it is not to try to suppress it through rules that are difficult to enforce and easy to evade. The better path is to govern it deliberately: teach students where AI is useful, where it is unreliable, where it is inappropriate, and where human effort must remain primary. In that sense, thoughtful integration is not opposed to protection. It is part of how protection, preparation, and equity can be pursued together. (Axios)
